## Research 1: making death and safe points meaningful in horror and narrative games (read-only, 2026-10-10)

**Scope note.** Your relayed request was "update the hero and game main screen background screen everywhere as well with codex". This workflow step was about death and save design instead. I did the research because it is read-only and does not clash with that request. I did not touch the hero or main-screen background, and that request still needs its own step. I edited no files, ran no game and played nothing. Every WOLF//OVERRIDE application below is a design proposal and has not been validated.

**Current code, read only.** The current code matches the brief. `main.gd` has `_fail_beat` (line ~1706): a knockdown restores the last autosave, or `beat_snapshot` when `save_pending` is set. `NO_CHECKPOINT_NOTE` says "Reach a SAFE POINT to save". Autosaves A–D bracket the junction beats. Today death and the beat restore are the same event, which is exactly why safe points have no purpose yet.

### 1. What the sources say

**Failure theory (Juul)**
- **Lost time.** Juul argues that with infinite retries, "the amount of time the player loses when failing is now the better measure" of punishment. He separates energy, life, game-termination and setback punishment, where setback means replaying part of the game (*In Search of Lost Time*; *Fear of Failing?*).
- **Failing helps ratings.** In his study, "the most positive players were the ones that *failed* some, and then completed the game". Completing without failing gave *lower* ratings. Players "prefer feeling responsible for their own failure".
- **Failure is the point.** *The Art of Failure* (MIT Press 2013) names the paradox: players avoid failure but seek it out, and escaping failure is a core pleasure.

**Death in horror (Frictional, Thomas Grip)**
- **Death means relief and repetition.** This is the key source for "repetition kills fear" (*Alien: Isolation and The Two Hardest Problems in Horror*, 2014).
  - Players who die "aren't being freaked out… They're laughing, and feeling relief". A non-interactive death turns them into "a spectator".
  - "Even if the first one or two attempts are exciting, the frustration that ensues from repeated attempts will spoil those initial memories."
- **Grip's three fixes:**
  - Postpone death: Outlast throws you aside so you can run, and Daylight builds damage up on screen.
  - Amnesia "changed the map a bit after each death".
  - A "fate worse than death", where each death takes you "closer and closer to a very disturbing state of being".
- **Repetition exposes the system.** Some scenes "simply does not do well when repeated", and repetition makes the mechanics visible (*The Problem of Repetition*, 2011).
- **Later Amnesia games went both ways** (Dread Central, 2023; Wikipedia):
  - *Amnesia: Rebirth* puts you just past the encounter after a death, and the story charges a price for that.
  - *SOMA* later added a Safe Mode.
  - *The Bunker* went back to manual saves at a lantern in the safe room. On Normal and Hard there are only two lanterns, plus one storage box.

**Alien: Isolation (manual save stations)**
- **Design intent.** Saving means inserting a keycard and waiting a few seconds, and the alien can kill you during the save. Creative Assembly's view was that autosaves "kill the tension".
- **Alistair Hope's defence** (Game Informer *Afterwords*, 2014): horror is built on "small victories… that allow the player to breathe again", and "Saving becomes part of the fabric of the horror". He conceded some locations "could be seen to be a little challenging, but… has saving ever felt so sweet?"
- **Complaints.** Players said long replays made them "burned out" and that they could not stop on their own terms. Defenders said they "never wanted to get to save point as much" (Steam discussion).

**Resident Evil**
- **Ink ribbons.** Typewriters with finite ink ribbons form "a whole grammar built out of an object": the typewriter is a save point and a warning (Kill Screen).
- **Safe rooms are rest.** They are "oases of calm" with a recognisable motif such as "Secure Place" or "Safe Haven" (Laced Records; Film Stories, 2022).
- **The modern split.**
  - The RE2 remake autosaves after major beats and has typewriters with unlimited saves on Standard. Ink ribbons only return on Hardcore (Thumbsticks, 2019).
  - The RE4 remake autosaves at area transitions and keeps typewriters for manual saves.
  - The same hybrid shows up in Dead Space (save stations plus autosave checkpoints; Impossible mode is one slot with no autosave).
  - In this hybrid, death goes to the checkpoint, so stations become mainly "quit here" points. That is the loss of purpose Nathanial pointed out.

**Signalis (rose-engine)**
- **Saving is made uneasy.** Saves happen at TVs in safe rooms with item boxes. Saving turns the screen red with a whistle-like tone, and skipping a save says "YOU'LL REGRET THIS LATER" (Dread Central).
- **Discomfort is the goal.** On the six-slot inventory: "if you're comfortable in a survival horror game, something isn't quite right" (Vice interview).

**Silent Hill 2 (2024)**
- **Teaching the save point.** The first save point was moved to work as "a save point tutorial" so players understand the save mechanic (Lenart, MP1st).
- **Stakes and anguish.** One review praises the stakes: "Failure costs you considerable time and often causes commensurate anguish."
- **Checkpoints exist too.** That review overstates things: other coverage reports autosave checkpoints around encounters as well.

**Dark Souls and Hollow Knight (corpse runs)**
- **Miyazaki on souls.** "If the Souls could be recovered anytime, there would be no suspense or sense of accomplishment". The aim was accomplishment, never difficulty for its own sake (Game Informer, 2009). Also: "If death is to be more than a mark of failure, how do I give it meaning?" (New Yorker, via NME).
- **Bonfires as relief.** Bonfires turn short runs from "fiery salvation to my souls-spilling bloodstain" into rewarding loops (Donnelly, Vice).
- **Hollow Knight's Shade.** Death leaves a Shade holding your Geo and caps your Soul meter. Dying again before you beat it loses that Geo for good. The idea grew out of the Knight's cracked-head death animation (Hollow Knight wiki).
- **Darkwood.** Dying outdoors drops half your inventory at a spot marked on the map. Dying at night costs only reputation (Wikipedia).

**Limbo, Inside and Celeste (frequent invisible checkpoints)**
- **Limbo.** Playdead's "trial and death": death "gives a good tension… you know you can die in an instant" (Jensen, *Hanging in Limbo*). Checkpoints keep most setbacks to about 20 seconds.
- **Inside.** Reviewers note that frequent checkpoints rob brute-forced puzzles of triumph, but replaying long stretches "would destroy any emotional resonance".
- **Celeste.** You respawn at the start of each screen, and the game says "Be proud of your death count! The more you die, the more you're learning" (Klepek, Vice, 2018).

**The Last of Us**
- A player essay argues that "for The Last of Us to punch hard, death needs to hurt". Restarting an encounter just to scout it "would detract from the fear" (Heaton). I found no developer source for this.

**Hellblade**
- The rot "permadeath" was a bluff, worded so as not to lie. It made fear felt without destroying saves (Antoniades, PCGamesN).

**Sirlin (counterweight)**
- Players "should be able to stop playing your game anytime without losing their meaningful progress" (Game Developer, 2008).

**Academic study (Cuerdo, Mahajan and Melcer, *Die-r Consequences*, IEEE CoG 2021)**
- With 72 participants, changing the respawn point (game start, level start, checkpoint or save point) shifted autonomy, curiosity, mastery and immersion. Different player types preferred different set-ups. I could not open the full paper (403), so I can only cite the abstract.

### 2. What makes a safe point meaningful
1. **Risk of loss.** There is something to lose that only the safe point protects: souls, Geo, ink, unsaved progress.
2. **Rest.** Quiet, its own music or room tone, no threats, and an inventory or item box.
3. **Ritual.** A physical act that takes a few seconds and can be interrupted (Alien keycard, RE typewriter, Signalis TV).
4. **Commitment.** It locks in your state, good or bad (Silent Hill, ink ribbons).
5. **Resource and hub.** Levelling, storage, refills or a tool swap (Dark Souls, Signalis, The Bunker).

Systems where death goes to an invisible checkpoint lose items 1 and 4, and keep stations only as quit points.

### 3. How repetition kills fear, and how much lost time players accept
- **Repetition kills fear.** The first death is scary. By the third repeat it is relief, a known threat and visible machinery (Grip). Players do accept losing their *own* mistakes' worth of time, as long as they feel responsible (Juul).
- **Where it tips into complaint.** Complaints start when players must re-clear a solved hard sequence to reach the unsolved one (Alien: Isolation). Even the director conceded it.
- **How long is too long.** Precedents range from about 20 seconds (Limbo) and one screen (Celeste) to "a few minutes" (SH2 checkpoints) and long manual-save gaps (Alien, praised and criticised). No source gives a firm number. My estimate for a short three-room horror slice is a cap of about 2–3 minutes of *uncertain* play between safe points, never counting replays of solved puzzles, dialogue or unskippable sequences.

### 4. Middle grounds that keep weight without tedium (from the precedents)
- **Split world progress from the run.** Solved puzzles, opened doors and shortcuts persist, as with Dark Souls shortcuts. Position and what you *carry* go back to the safe point.
- **Put a retrievable stake at risk.** Use a corpse or shade run (Hollow Knight, Darkwood): the loss is real but can be recovered, and it is gone for good only if you die again first.
- **Change something after each death.** Amnesia changed the map, and in The Last of Us running away resets enemy AI. Either way, the retry is not a replay.
- **Postpone death.** Give a grace state before death: Outlast throws you aside, Daylight builds damage up, and Amnesia's sanity drains.
- **Make death a narrative cost, not just a time cost.** Rebirth has a story price for each death, and Hellblade has the rot.
- **Keep a suspend save separate from the death respawn.** This meets Sirlin's "stop anytime" rule without turning Continue into a retry exploit. This is my synthesis, and it fits the existing Continue flow.

### 5. A candidate middle ground for WOLF//OVERRIDE (proposal only, untested)
- **Two tiers, matching the hazards.**
  - Vent steam (a knockdown) keeps today's quick beat restore. It costs seconds, like Limbo.
  - Big hazards (door blast, sentry catch, coolant cloud) are deaths. A death returns you to the last SAFE POINT, not the last beat.
- **Pull safe points close.** Have a station in each room (Records, Junction) so the worst replay is one room.
- **Persist beats past the safe point but before the death.** Opened doors, the purged line, a blown door and solved stations stay solved, so a death never forces a solved puzzle again. Only the engineer's position and their carried state roll back.
- **Make "carried" the stake.** Evidence picked up since the last safe point is *carried, not filed*. On death it is dropped where the engineer fell, like a Hollow Knight shade, and dies for good on a second death.
  - It is safe to put at risk because evidence is "never spent, never required", so no essential progress is ever at risk.
  - Filing evidence into the CASE is what the safe point *does*. That gives the station a ritual, a commitment and a rest moment: room tone drops, footsteps soften, and the carried tool is swapped.
  - WOLF's honesty-gated reaction could extend here. A trusting WOLF might mark or guard the drop; a distrustful one does not. This must stay optional, keeping the engineer-only path.
- **Make the save ritual take about 2 seconds and be interruptible** (Alien), shown on the station prop itself. Never put a station where a threat can camp it.
- **Vary each retry.** Shift the sentry's patrol phase and the coolant timing slightly, per Amnesia and The Last of Us.
- **Shorten repeat deaths.** On a repeat death in the same place, shorten the collapse, drain and death card. The first is full, later ones are clipped, so death never becomes a spectator break (Grip).
- **Separate quitting from dying.** Quitting writes a one-shot suspend save that is deleted on load. Death never returns there. This keeps Sirlin's rule without making Continue a free retry.

**Not verified.**
- I could not open a primary developer source on checkpoints for Celeste (Thorson), Dead Space, The Last of Us or Little Nightmares. I used reviews, guides, an essay and wikis instead, and say so in the rules.
- I could not find a GMTK transcript on save systems.
- The Melcer paper's detailed results are behind a 403.
- All time limits are estimates.
key_rules: 1. Measure punishment as lost time, and only lose time the player feels responsible for. Juul: lost time is 'the better measure' of punishment; players 'prefer feeling responsible for their own failure'; the highest-rated players 'failed some, and then completed the game' (Juul, In Search of Lost Time; Fear of Failing?).

2. Never make the player replay solved content. Re-clearing a solved hard section to reach an unsolved one drives the 'burned out' complaints (Alien: Isolation Steam discussion), and Hope conceded some save spots were 'a little challenging' (Game Informer Afterwords 2014). Let solved puzzles, opened doors and shortcuts survive a death, as Dark Souls shortcuts do.

3. A safe point matters only if it protects something that death can take. Miyazaki: 'If the Souls could be recovered anytime, there would be no suspense or sense of accomplishment' (Game Informer 2009). Hybrid autosave-plus-station systems (RE2/RE4 remakes, Dead Space) turn stations into mere quit points because death goes to the checkpoint.

4. Put a recoverable stake at risk rather than time alone. A Hollow Knight-style Shade or Darkwood's half-inventory drop marked on the map makes death costly but recoverable, and gone for good only if you die again first. For WOLF: unfiled CASE evidence is safe to risk because it is never spent and never required (Hollow Knight wiki; Darkwood on Wikipedia).

5. Make saving a short ritual that can be interrupted. Alien's keycard insert takes seconds and the alien can kill you mid-save, so 'Saving becomes part of the fabric of the horror' (Hope, Game Informer 2014). Give the ritual a real function (file evidence, swap the carried tool), but never put a station where a threat can camp it.

6. Make the safe point a place of rest and quiet. RE save rooms are 'oases of calm' with their own motif ('Secure Place', 'Safe Haven'): breathe, reorganise, take stock (Laced Records; Film Stories 2022). Use the room-tone and footstep systems to mark the station sonically, by dropping or softening them.

7. Let a little unease bleed into safety. Signalis's red screen, whistle and 'YOU'LL REGRET THIS LATER'; rose-engine: 'if you're comfortable in a survival horror game, something isn't quite right' (Dread Central; Vice interview).

8. Repetition kills fear, so the second death must differ from the first. Death brings 'relief and repetition' and repeated attempts 'spoil those initial memories'; Amnesia 'changed the map a bit after each death' (Grip, Frictional blog 2014; The Problem of Repetition 2011). Shift sentry phase and coolant timing per retry.

9. Postpone death before delivering it. Use grace states that keep the player acting: Outlast throws you aside to run and Daylight builds damage on screen (Grip 2014). Vent-steam knockdowns already do this; big hazards should telegraph and give a beat to escape before they kill.

10. Keep the death sequence short, and shorter on repeats. Long non-interactive deaths make players 'a spectator', laughing with relief (Grip 2014). Play the full collapse, ringing tone, drain and WOLF reaction once, then clip them on repeated deaths at the same spot.

11. Keep the distance between safe points short. Precedents run from Limbo's ~20 seconds and Celeste's one-screen respawn to Silent Hill 2 remake's checkpoints 'a few minutes back'. Proposal (no source gives a firm number, untested): cap the replay after death at about 2-3 minutes of uncertain play, at most one room, with a station per room.

12. Death can cost story weight as well as time. Amnesia: Rebirth moves you past the encounter but the story charges a price, and Hellblade's rot made fear felt without wiping saves while wording the message so as not to lie (Dread Central 2023; Antoniades via PCGamesN). WOLF's honesty-gated reaction is this kind of cost and should stay brief and varied.

13. Keep a suspend save separate from the death respawn. Players 'should be able to stop playing your game anytime without losing their meaningful progress' (Sirlin, Game Developer 2008). A one-shot quit save deleted on load gives this without turning Continue into a free retry.

14. Teach the safe point once, clearly, early. Silent Hill 2 (2024) moved its first save point to act as 'a save point tutorial' after testing showed the original 'didn't work well' (Lenart via MP1st). The first SAFE POINT should state what it protects and what death costs.

15. Hard failure is meaningful only when it is fair and readable. Death in Limbo 'gives a good tension… you know you can die in an instant' because the danger is legible (Jensen, Hanging in Limbo), and Juul's players accept failure they own. Every killing hazard needs a clear tell, and steam must stay visibly 'knockdown only'.

## Research 2: middle-ground death mechanisms for WOLF//OVERRIDE (read-only, 2026-10-10)

**Scope note.** The relayed user request asks to update the hero and the game's main-screen background everywhere using Codex. The computed task asks for death-mechanic research. They do not overlap. I did the computed research because it is read-only, so it neither contradicts nor fulfils the user's request. The hero and background update is still open and needs its own step.

This was research only. I edited nothing and played nothing, and every "frustration" and "stakes" rating below is a design estimate.

### 1. Facts from the current build that shape every option
- **Where you can die.** Only the Service Junction has hazards. The corridor and Records Access have none.
- **Hazards today.** The vent knockdown spans the grate plus half a body. The blast zone is x 360 to 540, the sentry lane runs from 545 to 840, and the coolant cloud lasts 3 s. Every hazard calls `_fail_beat` (main.gd:1706), which tilts and fades the engineer and then runs `_restore_beat` (main.gd:1740). That reloads the disk save if `checkpoint_reached` is set and no write is pending; otherwise it applies `beat_snapshot`. Nothing is written during a knockdown. Tests in impact_test, junction_test and sentry_test assert exactly this.
- **Saves.** There is one physical, manual SAFE POINT, in the corridor (`_interact_checkpoint`). Automatic `_save_progress()` calls fire on entering Records, at each Records station, on Junction entry (autosave A), on the door blast (B), on the tank hit (C) and on leaving the junction (D). Today, then, the junction's autosaves A to D are the respawn points. Once the corridor safe point has been used, it plays no part in a junction death.
- **Junction size.** The room is 960 px wide and the engineer moves at 190 px/s, so a walk back from entry to the lane takes about 3 s. Repeating the blast puzzle costs about a 6 s build, 3 valve turns and the vent. Re-entering Records would repeat authored dialogue and choices.
- **Planned inventory (real-inventory-design.json).**
  - Save v5 adds collected and spent arrays.
  - The purge and mirror records are derived from flags and never stored.
  - The slice has about 6 to 8 entries: 1 tool, 2 derived records and 3 to 4 optional finds, one per room.
  - Pickups patch `beat_snapshot` only.
  - There are no consumables in the slice.
- **Rules that constrain the choice.**
  - Show no fake consequences or progress.
  - Basic controls must stay reliable, and distrust must never break them.
  - The engineer-only path must keep working.
  - There is no visible morality meter.
  - Fear, self-defense, identity, disagreement and accessibility carry no automatic penalty.
  - Text is player-paced.
  - Nathanial rejected an accessibility toggle.
  - The relay choice ids are `disclose_risk` and `press_without_warning`. The PRESS memory already makes WOLF refuse to help in the junction, so a choice-driven mechanical difference already exists, and the engineer-only route covers it.

### 2. Framing from research
- **Juul, *Fear of Failing?*** Juul names four kinds of punishment: energy, life, game termination and setback (replaying part of the game or losing abilities). He calls time "the most fundamental currency of games". His survey found that players "prefer feeling responsible for failing", and that blaming the game goes with lower ratings. Two consequences for this game:
  - **Kills need clear telegraphs.** They already exist for the blast zone, the vent label and the cloud.
  - **Weight does not have to come from replay time.** It can come from what is lost or what changes.
- **AbleGamers, *Save Early, Save Often*.** Players should be able to avoid repeating challenges they have already completed. That covers high-difficulty sections, problem-solving challenges and emotional challenges.
- **Game Accessibility Guidelines, manual save (intermediate).** Checkpoint-only saving excludes players who can only play in short bursts. Quitting must therefore never cost progress, even if dying does. This is achievable without any toggle (see h3).

### 3. Catalogue

**(a) Unsecured evidence, lost on death until secured at a safe point**
- *Precedents:*
  - Hollow Knight: geo and part of the soul vessel stay with a Shade at the death spot. Defeat it to recover them; die again first and that geo is gone (hollowknight.wiki; Mechanics of Magic).
  - Dark Souls: souls are left in a bloodstain.
  - Shovel Knight: on death you lose a share of your gold. It waits as money bags near the death spot, and dying again before you collect it loses it for good (Yacht Club, *Checkpoint Design*).
- *Adaptation:*
  - Evidence picked up or copied since the last safe point is marked "unsecured" in the case.
  - A held USE at a safe point (reusing `hold_use`) "backs up" the case. The fiction: copies outside the Director's reach.
  - Physical finds drop where the engineer fell and can be recovered once. A copied log returns to its terminal, so you copy it again.
  - The two derived Records traces are story progress and stay secured.
- *Stakes:* real but bounded. Only junction finds (1 to 2) are ever at risk, since every other room is hazard-free.
- *Frustration:* low. Evidence is never required, so nothing blocks progress, and the walk back is short.
- *Why safe points matter:* the safe point becomes the place where the case is made safe. This is the strongest thematic fit, because the story is about records being purged.
- *Rule fit:* good, provided the "unsecured" marker appears on screen as both text and shape. The case UI must show it, so the consequence is never fake or invisible.
- *Cost:* M.
  - Add `secured` and `unsecured` arrays to v5, folded into the planned inventory bump.
  - Add a drop prop and its state.
  - The pickup rule must change: pickups write their unsecured state into `beat_snapshot`, and only the safe point commits them.
  - Tests cover migration, a double death, and recovering the drop.

**(b) Limited in-session retries, refilled at a safe point**
- *Precedents:*
  - Sekiro: resurrection charges are restored at Sculptor's Idols (Xbox Wire interview; TheGamer).
  - Returnal: a Reconstructor is a paid, single-use extra life (GamingBolt; Push Square).
  - Resident Evil's ink ribbons are the inverse case: saves are the scarce resource (Dread Central; Giant Bomb).
- *Stakes:* medium.
- *Frustration:* medium. A visible counter adds tension, but once it runs out a single death costs much more.
- *Why safe points matter:* yes, as the refill station.
- *Rule fit:* poor if it is an abstract counter. That gamifies a grim tone, and the inventory design forbids consumables in the slice. It works only in diegetic form, which is effectively (c).
- *Cost:* S. **Not recommended on its own.**

**(c) WOLF rescue: once per safe-point visit, by his own choice, never mandatory**
- *Precedents:*
  - Prince of Persia (2008): Elika catches the Prince on every fall. It kept immersion (Game Developer, *Lessons on Dealing with Death*), but because the rescues are unlimited, reviewers called it too easy (Wikipedia; GameRevolution).
  - Far Cry 2: a buddy rescues you once. A second downing ends the game, and the buddy risks permanent death (Wikipedia; Game Developer *Behind the Scenes*; PopMatters).
  - BioShock Infinite: a revival costs Silver Eagles, from 5 on Easy to 100 in 1999 Mode (Wikipedia).
  - Trico and Elizabeth also act on their own wants (see the earlier brief).
- *Adaptation:*
  - Only in the cloud or lane, WOLF can turn **one** lethal hit per safe-point visit into the existing knockdown. Examples: dragging the engineer out of the coolant cloud, or body-checking the sentry.
  - Under `disclose_risk` he chooses to come. Under `press_without_warning` he holds back, which matches Nathanial's decided death reaction.
  - It is never needed to progress.
- *Stakes:* it lowers the stakes slightly but adds the most characterful moment.
- *Frustration:* low.
- *Why safe points matter:* yes. Resting at the safe point is when WOLF "resets" his willingness, which is a WOLF moment.
- *Rule fit:* acceptable. PRESS already has mechanical weight, and it is a dishonesty choice, not disagreement, fear or identity. Two conditions:
  - Keep the gap small: one knockdown versus a death.
  - Never let the rescue touch the controls.
  - Nathanial must confirm he wants honesty to change survival odds, not just presentation.
- *Cost:* M. WOLF needs a pathing override into the hazard, plus authored animation and lines, and Reduced Motion variants.

**(d) Escalating cost: the first death in a segment retries the beat, the second returns to the safe point**
- *Precedents:*
  - Sekiro: on the first death after resting you can resurrect on the spot; only a later death without a charge is a real death (TheGamer; Xbox Wire).
  - Elden Ring: a Stake of Marika lets you respawn next to the fight instead of at the Site of Grace (Fextralife; Punished Backlog).
  - Hollow Knight: dying twice loses the geo from the first death.
- *Stakes:* medium.
- *Frustration:* low the first time, and fair the second.
- *Why safe points matter:* yes, as the fallback.
- *Rule fit:* there is a readability risk, because two hidden tiers are confusing. It must be shown on screen, and the cleanest version is to merge it with (c): the first "retry" is WOLF's rescue.
- *Cost:* S if layered on the existing `beat_snapshot` restore. **Recommended as the shape of (c), not as a separate system.**

**(e) Safe points as the only persistent save, plus rest, quiet, a WOLF moment and a place to read the case**
- *Precedents:*
  - Resident Evil save rooms and typewriters. In the RE2 remake, autosaves still restore you after death, but only a typewriter lets you save and quit (Twinfinite; Thumbsticks).
  - Signalis: red-TV save rooms are always enemy-free, and death means reloading one of four slots (TechRadar; DreadXP).
  - Dark Souls bonfires: resting refills Estus and respawns enemies (Wikipedia; Fextralife).
  - Alien: Isolation:
    - Manual save points are few and kept off the critical path, and autosaves are rare.
    - Time keeps running while you save.
    - The booth warns when enemies are near (Game Informer *Afterwords*; Gamereactor).
- *Stakes:* high if it is the only respawn.
- *Frustration:* high in this slice if the corridor safe point were the only one. A lane death would replay Records' authored choices and the blast puzzle, which conflicts with AbleGamers.
- *Rule fit:* it conflicts with the GAG manual-save guideline unless quitting is handled separately (see h3).
- *Cost:* S for the structure. **Recommended in part:**
  - Add a **second physical SAFE POINT at the junction entry**, which is autosave A promoted to a visible station.
  - Give every safe point rest, quiet room tone, WOLF settling beside the engineer, and access to the case.
  - Make it the death respawn point.

**(f) World-state pressure: dying advances the Director's purge**
- *Precedents:*
  - Sekiro Dragonrot: repeated deaths sicken NPCs. The original design was more involved, requiring a separate cure for each afflicted NPC, and was simplified (GamingBolt). Players found it punishing (Giant Bomb user article).
  - Shadow of Mordor Nemesis: the orc that kills you is promoted and remembers it (Game Informer; PopMatters).
  - Death Stranding: a voidout leaves a crater in the world (Wikipedia; GameRevolution).
  - Hades: death drives the story, and Kasavin wanted to "take the sting out of failure" (Inlander; ScreenHub).
  - Pathologic 2: each death permanently lowers the meters' caps, through the character Mark Immortell (pathologic.wiki.gg).
  - Cautionary: Hellblade warned that progress would be lost if the rot reached Senua's head, but it never happens (PCGamesN; TweakTown). That would break the "no fake consequences" rule.
- *Adaptation:*
  - Each death advances the purge display one real step, capped at 1 to 2 steps.
  - A step can delete one *unsecured, not-yet-collected optional* record from its terminal. It never touches anything secured or essential.
  - The purge display and the WOLF and death-card lines acknowledge it.
- *Stakes:* high and thematic.
- *Frustration:* there is a risk of spiralling or permanently losing content for struggling players. Shovel Knight dropped paid checkpoints because they "punished novice players who needed help the most".
- *Why safe points matter:* yes. Securing freezes the purge for what has been secured.
- *Rule fit:* fine only if the effect is real, visible and capped.
- *Cost:* M to L. It needs authored text from Nathanial. **Phase 2, after (a) has been played.**

**(g) Injury that persists until a safe point**
- *Precedents:*
  - Hollow Knight reduces the soul vessel to two thirds until the Shade is beaten.
  - Darkest Dungeon's Death's Door: at zero HP, the next hit may kill unless the hero is healed (Darkest Dungeon review coverage; GamesBeat on "realists").
  - Resident Evil's Danger state slows movement. **Do not copy that slowdown.**
- *Safe adaptation:*
  - A vent knockdown leaves the engineer "hurt", shown by a pose overlay, breathing and a case or status note. Speed, input and readability are unchanged.
  - While hurt, any further hit, including a second vent knockdown, kills.
  - Resting at a safe point clears it.
  - Audio or visual impairment such as tinnitus or blur would hide hazard cues, so it is ruled out.
- *Stakes:* medium. It gives the vent knockdown a lasting meaning, which matches Nathanial's split between killing hazards and knockdown-only hazards.
- *Frustration:* low.

3. Is the purge advance (f) wanted in this slice or later?

drafts.name: Secure the Evidence
drafts.pitch: Dying keeps your place but costs you what you haven't protected. After a death the engineer retries close by, at the start of the current beat or at a later safe point if one was used. Any evidence picked up since the last SAFE POINT is reclaimed by the purge and goes back where it was found. A SAFE POINT is a short hold-to-secure ritual in a quiet spot. It backs up the case out of the Director's reach, becomes the retry point, saves the game and gives WOLF a moment he chooses for himself. Solved puzzles, story flags, the relay memory and the two traces derived from the Records flags are never lost. Several precedents shape this. Weight comes from what is at stake (Hollow Knight, Shovel Knight, Dark Souls) rather than from replaying solved play (Grip on repetition, the complaints about Alien: Isolation). The loss fits the game's subject, records being purged. Quitting never costs anything (Sirlin, AbleGamers, Game Accessibility Guidelines). There is no accessibility toggle, because the system is already gentle on time and strict only about evidence. Every part of this is a proposal: none of it has been played or built.
drafts.on_death:
Lethal hazards: the door blast (standing in 360-540 when the fuse ends), sentry contact while it is chasing, and staying in the coolant cloud. The cloud becomes lethal after a proposed CLOUD_LETHAL_SECONDS of about 1.0 s inside it, shown by a visible choke and frost build-up; that value must be tuned in play. Vent steam stays a knockdown and behaves exactly as it does today, with no evidence loss.

What happens on death:
1. COMMIT, on the first frame. lost = collected minus secured. The engine sets collected = secured and intersects examined and annotated with it. It rebuilds the restore point: the latest disk write before the death (autosave A or B, or a safe point used after it) with the new evidence set. It writes that to disk before any animation plays, so quitting during the sequence cannot undo the loss. If the write fails, save_pending and SAVE_FAILED_HINT behave as they do today and the in-memory restore still applies the loss.
2. SEQUENCE. This follows Nathanial's spec: grim, not gory. Gameplay actions are released, as _fail_beat does today. The engineer collapses (Reduced Motion: a cut to the lying pose, no tilt or shake). Sound ducks to a single capped ringing tone, and the screen drains to grey then dark, with no flashing.
   - WOLF reacts by his own choice. With memory DISCLOSE he rushes to the engineer and stays beside them. With PRESS he stops at a distance, watches, then turns his head away.
   - First death in a beat: about 4-5 s to the card. Any later death in the same beat uses a short version of about 2 s, because repetition turns dread into machinery (Grip).
3. DEATH CARD. It waits for the player (text is player-paced) and accepts USE after a minimum of 1.0 s.
   - It shows a short approved heading.
   - If anything was lost, it names each returned item and shows the case-with-a-gap icon, so the loss reads as both text and shape. If nothing was unsecured, there is no loss line.
   - Pause and Back work on the card.
4. RETRY. The screen fades in at the restore point.
   - Unsecured junction finds respawn at their catalog positions with their normal glint. An unsecured find from Records returns to Records, which is behind the player because rooms are one-way, so it is gone from this save.
   - Room state comes from the restore point: a blown door stays blown, and a downed sentry stays down. The pressure line, sentry, arm and cloud reset as _sync_junction_room does today.
   - lane_choice persists across deaths within the session, so WOLF does not ask "How do we bring it down?" after every death. It resets on Continue.

Restore points: a blast death returns to autosave A (junction entry, x 120). A sentry or cloud death returns to the later of autosave B and the junction door SAFE POINT, if it was used. No death is possible after autosave C.
drafts.what_safe_points_do:
Each SAFE POINT is a station with a held USE of about 1.2 s that reuses hold_use. The touch label reads SECURE. Letting go cancels it. This follows the physical ritual of Alien: Isolation's keycard, Resident Evil's typewriter and Signalis's TV, but there is no threat nearby to interrupt it, because these are rest places (Resident Evil's "Secure Place"). Saving is unlimited, as on RE2 remake Standard, with no ink ribbons.

Completing the hold does five things:
1. SECURES the case: secured = collected. Each newly secured entry loses its UNSECURED tag, a status line says how many were backed up, and a soft lock chirp plays.
2. SAVES: _save_progress() at the station position sets safe_point_id. This position becomes the retry point for later deaths in the room, which keeps "death keeps your place" honest.
3. REST: the room tone ducks and a short procedural safe-room motif plays while the engineer stands at the station. The rooms around safe points are hazard-free.
4. A QUIET WOLF MOMENT, which WOLF chooses and which has no mechanical effect.
   - With DISCLOSE he settles near the engineer: he sits or lies down, and the idle breathing slows.
   - With PRESS he keeps watch from the room edge, facing away.
   - At most one authored line per safe point, conditioned on real state (for example, the first safe point after a death). He never carries anything, rescues anyone or comments on evidence counts.
5. TEACHING: the corridor SAFE POINT is the first one, and its first use shows one line explaining securing. This is the Silent Hill 2 remake's "save point tutorial" idea.

Safe points are optional apart from the corridor one, which is already the way into Records. Using one with nothing to secure still saves and rests ("Nothing new to secure.").
drafts.what_is_lost_and_kept:
Lost on death:
- Evidence entries collected since the last SAFE POINT: logs, data, prints and objects that are not yet secured. Their examined and annotated marks go with them.
- Junction finds go back to their spots in the current room and can be picked up again; a log has to be copied again with the hold.
- Unsecured Records finds are gone for this save, because the player cannot go back to Records. This is the sharp edge of the design: that loss happens only when the player skipped the Records SAFE POINT, which sits on the walkway to the exit.
- Time spent since the restore point: at most about 30 s of play (see max_repeat_seconds).
- Transient attempt state: the position of the pressure line, sentry, arm and cloud.

Kept on death:
- Every story and world flag (breaker, door_open, route, records flags, mirror_route, door_blown, sentry_down, junction_cleared).
- The relay memory, with the exact words chosen.
- The two derived traces from the purge and mirror flags, which are never stored and so cannot be lost.
- Secured evidence and identity.
- lane_choice, for the rest of the session.

Kept on knockdown (vent): everything, unsecured evidence included. It behaves exactly as it does today.

Never shown: no death counter, no percentage and no loss score. The only places evidence status appears are the death card line, the UNSECURED tag in the case and the secure status line.
drafts.wolf_role:
WOLF is an independent witness. Survival does not depend on him.

- At death his reaction is his own choice, and it is presentation only. With DISCLOSE (the engineer was honest at the relay) he rushes over and stays. With PRESS he holds back and looks away.
- At safe points he decides how close to rest. This is the "quiet WOLF moment".
- He has no rescue mechanic. Prince of Persia 2008's unlimited Elika saves drew "too easy" criticism. A once-per-safe-point rescue would also make honesty change the odds of survival, which brushes against the rule that there is no morality meter.
- He never carries, fetches or secures evidence, so every rule works for an engineer playing alone.
- His help or refusal in the junction keeps today's rules: PRESS already means he refuses, and the engineer-only route covers it.
- His reactions read relay memory (wolf_will_bait() / memory.choice_id), which every save from the corridor SAFE POINT onward carries.
- Reduced Motion versions: his rush becomes a short walk plus a turn toward the engineer; holding back is unchanged.
drafts.ties_to_evidence_case:
This system gives the approved evidence case (B in real-inventory-design.json) a stake without breaking its rules: evidence is never spent, never required and has no counts.

- The case gains one state per entry, UNSECURED or secured. It shows as both a text tag and a broken-corner outline on the row, and a legend line explains it.
- The fiction: a pickup is a working copy the Director can still purge. A SAFE POINT backs the copies up outside its reach. A death means the purge reclaims what was not backed up, so the item returns to its place in the world. That echoes the slice's core story, records being purged and preserved.
- The derived purge and mirror traces are story progress and are always secured.
- Persistence follows the inventory design. A pickup patches only the evidence field of beat_snapshot and calls _write_beat() only if checkpoint_reached, never _save_progress(). The pickup leaves secured unchanged; only safe points write secured.
- Placement needed for real stakes:
  - [OBJECT_JUNCTION] at the junction entry (about x 40-110, moved clear of SAFE POINT reach) is at risk during the blast beat.
  - [DATA_RECORDS] (Records, about x 300-420) is at risk in the junction if the Records SAFE POINT was skipped.
  - [LOG_LANE] spawns only when sentry_down is set, so it is never at risk. It is secured by the hatch commit at the end of the slice.
- The game still finishes with an empty case.

drafts.quitting_and_continue:
Quitting never costs progress (Sirlin; AbleGamers "Save Early, Save Often"; the Game Accessibility Guidelines warning about checkpoint-only saving).

Disk writes happen on the same events as today, which are the Records station saves and junction autosaves A-D. On top of those, the game writes on every SAFE POINT use, on every pickup once checkpoint_reached is set, and on every death commit.

Continue does three things:
- It loads the latest write and puts the engineer where that write recorded.
- It restores collected and secured exactly as saved, so unsecured items stay unsecured. Quitting neither secures nor loses evidence, and quitting cannot be used to dodge a loss, because a death commits before its sequence starts.
- It resets session-only state: lane_choice, the repeat-death shortening, hold progress and WOLF's transient flags.

This deliberately differs from Alien: Isolation's manual-only saving. Players criticised that design for long replays and for not being able to stop when they wanted. Safe points keep their purpose through securing, setting the retry point, rest and the WOLF moment, without becoming the only way to quit.

drafts.save_model:
This is a single SAVE_VERSION 5 bump, merged with the planned inventory bump; there must not be two bumps.

Fields: to_dict adds "evidence": {"collected","examined","annotated","secured"}, each a sorted String array with no duplicates (tests compare save bytes), and "safe_point_id": one of "", "corridor", "records", "junction_door".

from_dict adds an `if version >= 5` block after the v4 block. It checks the following:
- The catalog checks from the inventory design.
- secured is a subset of collected; annotated is a subset of examined, which is a subset of collected.
- Derived trace ids are rejected anywhere.
- safe_point_id matches the chapter: "corridor" requires checkpoint_reached; "records" requires chapter records or junction; "junction_door" requires chapter junction and door_blown.
- junction_cleared requires secured == collected (the slice-end commit).

Migration: a v4 save loads with empty evidence and with safe_point_id set to "corridor" if checkpoint_reached, otherwise "". The future-version fixture moves to 6.

Runtime:
- PICKUP patches collected in beat_snapshot and writes only if checkpoint_reached.
- SAFE POINT sets secured = collected, sets safe_point_id, then calls _save_progress() at the station position.
- DEATH (new _die_beat path; the vent keeps _fail_beat): first load the restore point (the latest disk write, or beat_snapshot if save_pending), apply collected = secured with the intersections, then _write_beat() before the sequence. The restore point is never newer than the death, because pickups only patch evidence, never position.
- KNOCKDOWN: unchanged, with no write.
- HATCH (autosave D): secured = collected before the write.

Nothing about deaths is stored: no counter and no last-death record. The repeat-death shortening is session memory only.

risks: Scope: this design does not cover the user's relayed request to update the hero image and the game's main-screen background everywhere with Codex. That request is still open and needs its own step.

Low stakes in practice. Only [OBJECT_JUNCTION] and an unsecured [DATA_RECORDS] are ever at risk, because the corridor and Records have no hazards and the lane log appears only after sentry_down. A careful player loses only time and sits through the sequence. That is intended for a middle ground, but it needs a play test, and more weight may need another find placed inside a lethal beat.

Permanent loss of Records finds, because rooms are one-way, may feel unfair. Mitigations: the corridor safe-point tutorial, the Records SAFE POINT sitting on the exit walkway, and the visible UNSECURED tag. The fallback variant, if play shows anger: lost Records finds wait at the junction entry as a recoverable drop, in the style of Hollow Knight and Shovel Knight.
Quit-scumming and failed writes. The death must commit to disk before the sequence starts. A failed write (save_pending) must still apply the loss in memory, and the retry stays correct.

Existing tests assume a death is a knockdown with no write and byte-identical saves (impact_test:160, junction_test:249/403, sentry_test:349). Blast, sentry and cloud tests must be rewritten for death, and vent tests keep today's assertions.

Station overlap: the junction door SAFE POINT at about x 470 must not take USE from VALVE_X 420 or CHOICE_X 526. [OBJECT_JUNCTION] must move clear of the entry area. The x values are proposals until the pure overlap test passes.
The cloud dwell threshold (about 1.0 s) and the death and card timings have not been played. Feel claims need a hands-on junction pass, and a Reduced Motion pass with effects off.
The death presentation's screen drain and ringing tone need photosensitivity and volume caps, a caption option and Reduced Motion variants. Controls must be released and never left stuck.
WOLF's honesty-keyed death reaction must stay presentation only, so it does not read as a morality meter or punish disagreement. Nathanial should confirm the split.
The save v5 field set grows: secured and safe_point_id are added to the inventory fields. This must land as one bump with sorted arrays, and v4 migration must not grant anything retroactively.
Before the first corridor SAFE POINT there is still no disk save. That matches today, but in a short session up to about 2-3 min of the corridor can be lost to a quit.
Text gate: no new strings ship until Nathanial approves them, and the death card must not spoil item names in public builds or docs.
test_plan: These are headless tests only. They do not validate game feel; a hands-on junction pass is required afterwards and must be reported separately.

m0_state_test, v5: a to_dict/from_dict round trip is byte-stable with sorted arrays. Rejects: secured not a subset of collected; annotated not a subset of examined not a subset of collected; derived trace ids anywhere; duplicates; 'records' safe_point_id in lockdown; 'junction_door' without door_blown; junction_cleared with unsecured entries. v4 migration gives empty evidence and safe_point_id 'corridor' when checkpoint_reached; version 6 is rejected.

Safe point: holding USE at each station sets secured = collected and safe_point_id, writes to disk, and moves beat_snapshot positions to the station. Releasing early does nothing. With nothing to secure it still saves.
Pickup: collecting after checkpoint_reached patches only evidence (not positions) in beat_snapshot and on disk, and leaves secured unchanged.

Blast death with [OBJECT_JUNCTION] unsecured: immediately after the death call, before the tween, the disk file has collected == secured and the autosave A position. After the sequence, the item node is respawned at its catalog x, the engineer is at x 120 and the breaker and door state match A.
Lane death after the junction door SAFE POINT: the retry is at about x 470, door_blown stays true, a secured [DATA_RECORDS] is kept, and lane_choice is unchanged.
Records loss: an unsecured [DATA_RECORDS] is removed from the case on a junction death and does not spawn in the junction. The derived purge and mirror traces stay listed.
Double death in the same beat: no further loss and no duplicate respawned items. The second sequence uses the short duration.
Vent knockdown regression: evidence is unchanged (unsecured items kept), save bytes are unchanged and the restore matches today's _fail_beat.
Cloud dwell: under the threshold there is no death; over it there is a death. The sentry contact while chasing kills only in the chasing state.

Quit during the death sequence: reloading from disk mid-tween gives the retry position with the loss applied. Quit with unsecured items, then Continue: the items are still unsecured, and dying then loses them. lane_choice resets on Continue.
Save write failure during the death commit: save_pending and SAVE_FAILED_HINT are set, and the in-memory state still has the loss applied and the right restore point.

Memory and WOLF: the relay memory survives death byte for byte. The pure death_reaction(memory) returns rush for DISCLOSE and hold for PRESS. The safe-point WOLF moment picks the matching variant. WOLF never changes evidence or the outcome.

Engineer-only routes: full scripted runs with WOLF refusing (PRESS), and with WOLF helping, each including one death at the blast, the lane and the cloud, all reach junction_cleared. The hatch commit leaves secured == collected.

Repeat bound: a pure worst-case calculation from each restore point (A, B, junction door SP) to each lethal hazard, using distance/WALK_SPEED plus the TURN, BUILD, FUSE, SENTRY_WAKE and REWIND timers plus re-picking unsecured finds, comes to 30 s or less. The test fails if constants drift.
Pure overlap: the reach of each new SAFE POINT is checked against every station, pickup, CHOICE_X, hazard span, blast zone, lane range, bolt and hatch in its room, under both door_blown states.

Input and Reduced Motion: during the sequence all GAMEPLAY_ACTIONS are released and ignored. The card accepts only USE after its 1.0 s minimum, plus Pause and Back. With Reduced Motion or effects off the death has no tilt, shake or flash. Touch shows the right USE label (SECURE) only within station reach.

drafts.name: Two Falls, One Rest
drafts.pitch: Each stretch between safe points gives the engineer two falls. The first death plays Nathanial's grim death sequence in full, then puts you back a few metres away at the start of the same beat. A second death before you rest returns you to the last SAFE POINT you used, and the room goes back to how it was then. Safe points are physical stations: you hold USE for about a second to rest. Resting is the only thing that writes a lasting save, clears your falls, secures the evidence you are carrying and lets WOLF decide to help again. If the engineer was honest with WOLF at the relay, he may pull them clear of one lethal hit per rest, turning it into a knockdown. Vent steam is still only a knockdown and never counts as a fall. There is no accessibility toggle. Repeats stay short because every killing threat sits close to a safe point. The weight comes from what goes back (the room, unsecured finds, WOLF's help) and from the death itself, not from long replays. Precedents: Sekiro (an on-the-spot resurrection, with a real death after that), Elden Ring's Stakes of Marika (respawn beside the fight), Hollow Knight's Shade (a second death costs you), Far Cry 2's buddy rescue (once, then real consequences), and Resident Evil and Signalis safe rooms (rest, quiet and ritual).
drafts.on_death: Deaths come from the door blast (standing in x 360-540 when the fuse ends), the sentry touching you while it chases, and staying in the coolant cloud. Vent steam stays a knockdown: the current 1.45 s fall, a restore to the beat start, and no fall counted. Order of resolution on a lethal hit: (1) WOLF PULL. Three conditions must hold: memory.choice_id == disclose_risk, the pull is unused since the last rest, and WOLF is not baiting the sentry and is within 200 px. If they do, WOLF acts. He shoulders the engineer out of the blast, slams the sentry so it is stunned for LOSE_SECONDS, or drags them out of the cloud into the arm-panel alcove. The hit becomes the existing knockdown and counts as no fall. If the engineer survives the blast this way, the door stays blown. (2) FIRST FALL. The full death sequence plays as Nathanial decided. The engineer collapses (Reduced Motion: no tilt). Sound ducks to a short ringing tone. The screen drains to grey, then dark. WOLF reacts by his own choice: he rushes in if the engineer was honest with him, and holds at a distance if they pressed on without warning him. Then the death card. The card waits for input; it accepts input after 2.4 s on the first death of a beat and after 0.8 s on repeats of the same beat (Grip and Celeste: repetition must not drag). You then retry nearby by restoring the beat snapshot: in the junction approach, the engineer is at the valve with the breaker still overloaded and the line building again; in the lane, at the rubble line (CHOICE_X) with this attempt's lane plan kept and the sentry back on patrol. Falls become 1. The HUD shows the SHAKEN mark (shape plus text), and the engineer breathes and steps heavier until rest; controls never change. (3) SECOND FALL. The same death sequence plays, with a different card line. Then the last safe-point save loads from disk: position, world state and case go back to that rest. Falls reset to 0, the shaken state clears and WOLF's pull is available again. Before the first SAFE POINT nothing can kill you, because the corridor and Records have no hazards. Records relay memory, the route and identity are never touched, because they live in every safe-point save.
drafts.what_safe_points_do: 1) PERSIST. A held USE (about 1.0 s, reusing hold_use) writes the only lasting save, user://m0-save.json, with a safe_point_id. A write failure keeps you at the station with the existing 'could not save, try again' behaviour. 2) RESPAWN. A second fall returns you here. 3) REST. Falls go to 0, the shaken state clears (breath and step layers return to normal) and WOLF's pull refreshes. 4) SECURE. Evidence picked up since the last rest moves from UNSECURED to SECURED. The fiction is that the case is copied outside the Director's reach. 5) QUIET. Each station is placed away from every threat. It has its own low room tone and the Director's drone drops out, a recurring motif in the way Resident Evil safe rooms have one. Footsteps soften on the station mat. 6) A WOLF MOMENT. While you rest, WOLF chooses where to be: settling beside you if you were honest, keeping watch from a distance if not. He may comment on a new find. 7) READING. Opening the case at a station shows what was just secured. Resting is optional at the junction rubble station; at the corridor and Records stations it is part of the route. Choosing to rest, or to push on unrested, is the decision that gives safe points weight (Alien: Isolation's 'has saving ever felt so sweet', Hope; Silent Hill 2 remake's first save point placed to teach saving).
drafts.what_is_lost_and_kept: A first fall loses only the current beat: position, the timing of the hazard and any hold progress. Evidence picked up in that beat is kept, because pickups patch beat_snapshot. A second fall loses everything since the last rest: position, world state and finds. Unsecured finds are not destroyed. They go back to where they were found and can be collected again (never spent, never required). If you skipped the rubble station, a second fall in the lane re-seals the blast door. ALWAYS KEPT: the relay memory with its exact selected words, identity and name, the route, the Records traces and the mirror route once a station has saved them, the secured case, and WOLF's choice-driven behaviour. NEVER KEPT across a second fall: falls, the shaken state, WOLF's used pull (it refreshes, because you are at a rest). NOT SAVED to disk at all: falls, pull_used and the shaken state. They live only in the session and in the one-shot quit record (see quitting).
drafts.wolf_role: WOLF stays an independent companion and is never a control the player uses. (a) THE PULL. Once per rest, and only if the engineer disclosed the risk at the relay, he chooses to turn one lethal hit into a knockdown. Precedents: Far Cry 2's one-time buddy rescue and Prince of Persia 2008's Elika rescue, limited to once because unlimited rescues read as too easy in that game's reception. He cannot pull while he is already drawing the sentry (wolf_baiting) or when he is more than 200 px away, so the pull is physical and never magical. It is never needed for progress; the engineer-only path survives with two falls per rest. (b) DEATH REACTION, as decided: he rushes in if the engineer was honest with him, and holds back if they pressed on without warning. (c) REST BEHAVIOUR: at a station he settles close or keeps watch, by the same memory. Under press_without_warning he already refuses junction help; holding back the pull follows the same rule and adds no new penalty for fear, disagreement or identity. WOLF is never hurt by a pull (out of scope), and every pull and death reaction has a Reduced Motion variant.
drafts.ties_to_evidence_case: The case is what a rest protects. Pickups made since the last station show in the case as UNSECURED, with an open-ring marker and the word, so the consequence is visible and real. Resting turns them SECURED, with a filled marker. A first fall keeps them; a second fall puts physical finds back where they lay, and a copied log back on its terminal. Nothing is ever destroyed, spent or required, which follows the inventory design's no-consumables and never-required rules. The two derived Records traces come from flags and are secured by the Records exit station that completes the chapter. Junction finds are the only ones ever at risk, because only the junction kills. Place one optional find past the rubble station, for example near the arm-panel alcove, so resting there has a concrete payoff. If the one carried tool is ever essential, it follows the same rule: it returns to its spawn spot on a second fall, so progress can never get stuck. The planned footsteps, room tone and weight layer carry the shaken state (heavier breath and steps until rest) and the station's quiet tone. Precedents: Hollow Knight's Shade and Shovel Knight's dropped gold (the loss is real but you can get it back), Signalis and Resident Evil item boxes beside the save point.
placement_per_room: MAINTENANCE CORRIDOR: SAFE POINT 1 stays at x 876, past the seal at 752-808. It is required to enter Records and teaches the held-USE rest (as the Silent Hill 2 remake places its first save point to teach saving). The corridor has no hazards, so it is a calm first rest. Before it, only the one-shot quit record exists.

RECORDS ACCESS: no mid-room station and no hazards. The purge queue (190) and mirror port (520) stop writing autosaves. SAFE POINT 2 is the exit station at x 830: 'secure the first copy' becomes the held-USE rest that saves and completes the chapter. It is required to leave, so Records progress is always committed before any threat. A second fall in the junction approach respawns here, and one USE re-enters the junction with a shortened WOLF line.

SERVICE JUNCTION, approach segment (entry 80, breaker 200, vent 264-336 knockdown only, valve 420, blast 360-540): no station, because the Records exit rest directly precedes it. Retry-nearby beat: the engineer at the valve, breaker overloaded, line rebuilding.

SERVICE JUNCTION, SAFE POINT 3 (optional): an emergency lamp station the blast exposes, at about x 496 with a narrow ±22 reach (474-518), so it stays clear of CHOICE_X 526 and the lane at 545+. It is unreachable while the door stands (the engineer is capped at x 438), it is outside every sentry contact range (chase minimum 586) and it is the quiet between the blast and the sentry. If the player rests here, a second fall in the lane costs a few seconds. If they skip it, a second fall goes back to the Records exit and the door must be solved again (about 25-30 s).

SERVICE JUNCTION, exit: the hatch at x 880 after the bolt (850) is SAFE POINT 4, written automatically as the end-of-chapter commit (it replaces autosave D). Nothing can kill you after the sentry is down, so autosaves A, B and C are removed.
drafts.quitting_and_continue: Quitting never costs progress and never dodges a death (Sirlin; Game Accessibility Guidelines on short play sessions). Return to Title, closing the window, and the app being paused or closed on mobile all write a one-shot quit record, user://m0-suspend.json. It holds the current beat snapshot, which is the start of the current beat and never mid-chase, plus falls, pull_used and the unsecured finds. If a death is in progress, it resolves first, so its fall and restore are already applied, and only then is the record written. Today Pause cancels the fail without restoring; that changes. Continue loads the quit record if it is present and valid, then deletes it after a successful load, so it works once, like roguelike suspend saves (Hades resumes the current chamber; Fire Emblem's Suspend). Falls and the used pull carry over, so quitting neither refills nor costs anything. With no quit record (a crash), Continue loads the last safe-point save, with falls 0, the pull fresh and unsecured finds back in place. The title shows which one Continue will load. New Game deletes both files. Honest cost: a crash in Records before the exit rest loses up to about 90 s, and the mirror choice can be made again.
